title: Losing face? Licensing and governing AI content in China
gist: China's booming AI microdrama industry pays ordinary people US$15-700 for one-time facial-likeness licensing, but the licenses are unbounded — a face licensed once could be reused indefinitely across unlimited future content — exposing a regulatory gap between China's existing portrait-rights/biometric law and generative AI's ability to make a face a reusable, monetizable asset.

insights.claim: In China, people are being paid between US$15 and US$700 to license their facial likenesses for use in AI-generated microdramas and advertisements produced for mobile viewing.
insights.speaker: Haiqing Yu
insights.so_what: A new labor/IP market is forming around biometric likeness licensing at very low price points, which could scale into a significant informal labor category and a governance/liability exposure for AI content platforms.
insights.quote: people are paid from between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses for AI-generated microdramas and advertisements produced for mobile phone viewing
insights.locator: opening paragraphs citing Rest of World report

insights.claim: More than 95% of microdramas released in China in the first three months of 2026 reportedly used AI somewhere in their production, reflecting near-total AI penetration of this fast-growing mobile entertainment format.
insights.speaker: Haiqing Yu
insights.so_what: Near-saturation AI adoption in microdrama production signals this content format as a leading indicator for where generative AI production tooling scales fastest — relevant for AI content-tooling investment theses.
insights.quote: More than 95% of microdramas released in China during the first three months of 2026 reportedly used AI somewhere in their production.
insights.locator: paragraph on China's mobile entertainment industry

insights.claim: A single facial-licensing agreement authorizing one advertisement leaves open whether the same AI facial model could later appear in 100 different ads, a romance or political drama, or be aged, sexualized, or scripted to say things the person never would.
insights.speaker: Haiqing Yu
insights.so_what: This is the core governance gap: licensing scope, duration and downstream-use limits are undefined, creating open-ended reputational and legal liability for licensors and platforms alike.
insights.quote: An agreement might authorise one advertisement. But could the same AI facial model later appear in 100 advertisements? A romance or a political drama? Could it be aged, sexualised or made to say things you would never say?
insights.locator: paragraph on licensing and new AI governance problem

themes.theme: Three modes of 'the face' and why generative AI changes the calculus

insights.claim: A face now operates in three distinct registers simultaneously: as social identity (reputation/status), as biometric identifier (authentication, surveillance, payments), and, newly through generative AI, as a reproducible digital asset detachable from the body.
insights.speaker: Haiqing Yu
insights.so_what: A useful mental model for classifying facial-data regulation: privacy/biometric rules (identification) do not automatically cover the separate economic-rights problem of reusable AI likeness (what the face can be made to do).
insights.locator: section on the face operating in three ways

insights.claim: Facial recognition technology answers 'who is this person?' while generative AI answers 'what can this face do?' — a shift from identification governance to a governance problem about reusable, monetizable digital assets.
insights.speaker: Haiqing Yu
insights.so_what: Regulators and platforms building AI governance frameworks need distinct rules for asset-reuse rights, not just biometric privacy protections; a template gap likely exists in other jurisdictions besides China.
insights.quote: Facial recognition is primarily concerned with identification, “who is this person?” Generative AI asks, “what can this face do?”
insights.locator: section on facial recognition vs generative AI

insights.claim: When a face becomes a reusable AI asset, its economic value is not exhausted by the initial one-off licensing fee — repeated commercial use across ads, dramas and platforms accrues ongoing value that flows to AI firms, studios and distributors rather than the original licensor.
insights.speaker: Haiqing Yu
insights.so_what: Points to a value-capture asymmetry investors in AI content platforms should note: current licensing structures may understate future liability/royalty obligations if renewed-consent or revenue-share rules are eventually mandated.
insights.quote: A modest one-off payment may enable repeated commercial use across advertisements, dramas and platforms, while the resulting value rests with AI firms, studios and distributors.
insights.locator: paragraph on value versus privacy question

themes.theme: China's existing legal architecture and its gaps

insights.claim: China's Civil Code already grants portrait rights as part of personality rights, and its 2025 Measures on the Security Management of Facial Recognition Technology Applications (effective 1 June 2025) define facial information as protected biometric data, while the Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services (effective August 2023) link generative AI to personal-information and data-security law — yet none of these directly addresses indefinite reuse of a licensed AI facial model.
insights.speaker: Haiqing Yu
insights.so_what: Investors/operators in China's AI-content space should expect near-term regulatory tightening specifically targeting reuse scope and duration, since existing law covers consent-at-capture but not consent-over-time.
insights.locator: section on China's existing laws governing faces

insights.claim: A meaningful licensing framework for AI facial likeness should specify permitted uses, duration and scope, prohibit sensitive uses, enable traceability, and require renewed consent or further payment for continued commercial use.
insights.speaker: Haiqing Yu
insights.so_what: A concrete regulatory template that Chinese authorities (or other markets facing the same gap) are likely to move toward — a leading indicator for compliance requirements AI content companies may soon face.
insights.locator: concluding paragraphs on what licensing frameworks should specify
